Donkey Slaughter

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate the brutal slaughter of hundreds of donkeys in the rising trade in donkey skins

Unique Selling Point:
South African donkeys are being stolen, trafficked, brutally bludgeoned and skinned alive to feed the Chinese demand for donkey skins. The skin is sought after for the gelatin which is believed to have anti-ageing properties and is a key ingredient in E'jiao tonic. We go to a donkey auction in the Northern Cape where thousands has been donated to o the Karoo Donkey Sanctuary to bid on the auction and transport the donkeys to safety.

Summary:
The SPCA raised a house in Benoni and recovered 5000 donkey skins. Each skin is worth R7000. They also arrested and charged two men in Oligantshoek who had brutally bludgeoned hundreds of donkeys to death with a hammer.

Extra Budget Items:
Flight tickets to Kimberley
Car hire to drive to Hartswater to the auction.

Press Release:


Donkeys in Demand
This week’s discovery of more than 5 000 donkey hides in a container in Benoni has shed light on the illegal slaughter and trade in the animals for meat and skin, allegedly by a Chinese syndicate. With hides said to sell for up to R7000 each, Carte Blanche investigates the trade in local donkeys purportedly for use in Chinese medicine, and estimated to be worth millions.


Script:


DONKEY SLAUGHTER

V/O: 350 donkeys are going on auction in the Northern Cape. Never before has this sale yard in Hartswater been the focus of so much media attention. But the recent spike in donkey killing has caused a national outcry.

Grace: Last year the Polokwane SPCA intercepted a truck that was travelling from the Limpopo province to Gauteng, and it had 41 donkeys on it. Some were adults and some were foals. The conditions on this truck were absolutely horrendous. The donkeys were trampled, some of them were dead, some of them were busy dying, all in the name of this horrific trade.

V/O: Grace de Lange manages the Farm Animal Protection Unit of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.

Bongani: How bad is the situation?

Grace: It’s very bad; we are starting to get reports on a weekly basis of animals that are being transported, animals that are being slaughtered in the most horrendous manners.

Bongani: What has driven this sudden interest in donkey skins?

Grace: We are informed that the skins are sent to China, they are used for medicinal purposes, and we’ve been informed they are getting high prices, something like seven and a half thousand rand per skin.

Link: From the Bible to Shakespeare, donkeys have been part of human life for centuries. Commonly thought of as beasts of burden who suffer in silence they haven’t always been of much value – until now.

Jonno: I was up in Polokwane recently, chatted to a Chinese gentlemen that confirmed to me that between 15 and 20 thousand donkeys have been slaughtered between Polokwane and Musina on the Zim border in the last 6 months. So the trade is massive.

V/O: Jonno Sherwin from the Karoo Donkey Sanctuary in Prince Albert is also at the auction.

Jonno: The requirement in China for donkeys to produce E’jiao, which is the tincture they use that this is all about, their requirement is about 8 million donkeys annually, completely unsustainable. China is able to supply in the region of 3 million donkeys, the balance is sourced from all over the world. It has now hit us in a big way.

Bongani: What do they use the donkey skins for?

Jono: We believe they boil the skins and the gelatin rises to the surface that is then used to make a tincture.

Kelly: Traditionally we use E’jiao to improve the body’s health condition to tonic the blood, to help assist to stop the bleeding and also to nourish the yin energy. But in the Chinese medicine field there are many other plant based Chinese herbal medicines that can do the same job, or even better.

V/O: Dr Kelly Kong May is a doctor of traditional Chinese medicine, registered with the Health Professions Council.

Kelly: The way the donkeys are being killed, we are totally not agree with that.

Bongani: Is E’jiao legal to use in South Africa?

Kelly: Our Chinese medicines we use are plant-based. So we don’t use animal-based material in South Africa.

V/O: But that’s the registered doctors. We went shopping undercover in Joburg’s Chinatown, and since E’Jiao isn’t illegal it was openly available.

Shop 1: They say this per one kilo, maybe ten thousand rands per one kilo.

Shop 2: You see, one piece four hundred.

Shop 3: Two thousand eight hundred.

V/O: And it is this promise of profit that is driving the demand for donkey skins. Ashley Ness runs the Highveld Horse Care Unit. She initiated the recent raid on a plot near Benoni.

Ashley: I got sent a photograph of skins that were being dried. I called members of the stock theft unit. We were let in by a Chinese individual who obviously claimed to not know anything. From the photograph we matched the scenery, found the shed, found the container.

Bongani: What was in it?

Ashley: A massive pile of donkey skins.

V/O: It’s estimated there were almost 5000 donkey skins salted, dried and ready for export.

Ashley: The clearing agents are registered, and they are applying for clearance through SARS. And on these clearance certificates it says “donkey skin’.

V/O: Once the clearance certificate is received the containers are allegedly shipped to Hong Kong.

Link: It’s estimated that thousands of donkeys have already been killed across the country, and if the Benoni bust is anything to go by, many of their skins have left in containers just like this. Certainly the monitoring of these exports leaves much to be desired.

V/O: Documents seized in Benoni show that some of the donkeys were from a village in Limpopo.

Grace: People are approached to buy their donkeys, and if they refuse the villagers find that a few weeks down the line, that their animals have been left in the field, they’ve been brutally slaughtered, and the skins are missing.

V/O: A donkey skin reportedly sells for between two and three thousand rand locally. So much like rhinos, donkeys are now being poached and illegally slaughtered in the bush. The implements are crude, the methods cruel. A leaked video shows kids and dogs milling about before this gentle, trusting creature is ruthlessly bludgeoned and skinned. We cannot show you the rest as it is too horrendous to watch.

Grace: Recently in Olifantshoek two men were arrested that were using a sledgehammer to hit the head of the donkeys and then skinning them alive.

V/O: More than a hundred donkeys were massacred in this way, their smashed skulls bearing the trauma of the blows. They were then skinned and butchered with saws and axes. Two suspects‚ Dawid Pappie and Heinrich Smit‚ were charged and released on bail. They will appear in the Kathu Magistrate’s Court on February the 16th.

Link: There is no denying the demand for these animals, it is said to be the biggest donkey auction ever, and the anticipation is already building as they are being moved from their various pens, and all around us, all we can see are donkeys.

Jonno: Essentially none of these donkeys are really in fit condition to work, so we imagine that the equine abattoirs will be here to bid on them, against ourselves.

Bongani: What will they do with the donkeys?

Jonno: They will slaughter the donkeys – hopefully in a humane manner.

V/O: Jonno alerted the public to the auction on Facebook. Now he’s here to rescue donkeys with crowd-funding, and a racehorse carrier.

Bongani: So for you the sounds we are hearing aren’t just normal donkey sounds?

Jonno: No those are mares calling for their babies. They were all separated by the auctioneer this morning because they’re going to be selling them off in separate stock lots. Baby as one, moms as another. Those are the moms screaming for their babies.

Link: The auction has begun in earnest. We’re told there are a number of bidders here, and we’re told they quite prepared to spend a lot of money. The question is, can Jono and his donkey sanctuary outbid them?

Bidding Sfx

V/O: A few years ago a donkey cost between four and five hundred rand. At the auction the donkeys were fetching well over R2 000 each. That’s more than an impala or a blue wildebeest.

Bongani: Jonno how did it go today?

Jonno: So we bought 130 donkeys and I think we’ve bought about 20 horses.

V/O: This weekend the foals arrived at the Sanctuary and were reunited with their moms. All the donkeys are now under armed guard while they settle in and wait to be re-homed.

Bongani: Aren’t you in a sense postponing the inevitable?

Jonno: Not necessarily; at least we are saving a hundred lives. We feel that’s enough to create the awareness that we want to create to stop all of this.
